newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION - Ifo's view of Spanish economy in 1997, 1998.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Ifo's view of Spanish economy in 1997, 1998.

text.p: By Dr. Oskar-Erich Kuntze, an economist specialising in industrial countries and European integration at Germany's Ifo economic institute.

Economic growth in Spain picked up only slightly during 1996. Real GDP grew by 2.2 percent mainly stimulated by the still undervalued exchange rate of the peseta, the economic recovery in Western Europe and declining interest rates. Fiscal policy was restrictive. Exports (plus 10.3 percent) and investment in plant and machinery (plus 6.1 percent) were the main driving forces while private consumption (plus 1.9 percent) was rather sluggish.

Public consumption stagnated and construction dropped by 2.3 percent. The situation in the labour market improved in the course of the year, bringing the unemployment rate down by 0.7 percentage points to 22.2 percent. Consumer prices increased by 3.6 percent with very modest inflation during the year. The current balance showed an enlarged surplus of Pts 224 billion also due to improved terms of trade.

Economic policy will continue to be supply-side oriented by speeding up liberalisation, deregulation and privatisation in a very pragmatic way and by achieving a widespread consensus. In 1997, priority will be given to meeting the Maastricht criteria as far as possible. Along these lines fiscal policy will keep its restrictive stance in 1997 but will loosen it somewhat in 1998.

On the other hand, monetary policy will stimulate the economy in 1997 and well into 1998; in the run-up to 1999, interest rates might start rising. There are strong intentions to keep the exchange rate of the peseta as stable as possible within the European Monetary System.

In 1997, economic activity will continue to pick up bringing the growth rate of real GDP to roughly 3 percent with exports (in first place) and gross fixed investment as the main driving forces. While public consumption might stagnate further on, private consumption will gain momentum. The situation in the labour market continues to improve. All in all, inflation is likely to be moderate. Consumer prices might increase by almost 2.5 percent. In the current balance, a surplus can once more be expected.

In 1998, economic growth is likely to strengthen further with exports and gross fixed capital formation still the most dynamic forces. Private consumption might pick up further and public consumption should revive. Real GDP can be expected to grow by 3 percent to 3.5 percent. The situation in the labour market will improve noticeably. Inflation will accelerate somewhat bringing the inflation rate (CPI) to around three percent. The current balance might slip slightly into the red.
Monitoring the "Maastricht capability" of Spain, the findings are that concerning consumer prices, interest rates, and exchange rate stability the criteria are very likely to be met in 1997.

Even the threshold of the public deficit (3 percent in relation to GDP) will probably be achieved. But concerning public debt, the Maastricht criterion will be missed significantly, though not as much as by the majority of the EU countries.

Public finance is nevertheless the crucial point, firstly, because of various and significant examples of "creative accounting" and other measures designed to bring down the public deficit (in relation to GDP), and secondly, because there is no indication that the public debt (in relation to GDP) is sufficiently declining. The Spanish government has recently announced a convergence programme for 1998 to 2000, promising a further drop of the public deficit and a reduction of the public debt by the year 2000.

In order to provide evidence that there is really something in this intention of continuing the consolidation of public finance -- without creative accounting etc -- a prolongation of the reference period at least up to the year 1998 is be recommended.
